messages.subject: BYM model with more rows than polygons
messages.subject_clean: BYM model with more rows than polygons
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I have data from a poll conducted in a sample from public hospitals across the country, in which people were asked whether they had a certain disease and different covariates such as weight, age, sex, etc. The number of people polled in each hospital is not constant, and I'm trying to fit a BYM model using the data from each individual without summarizing it per polygon. This means that I have more rows in the data frame than polygons, with a column named ID that indicates where does each row belong to.

I tried using the following formula:
>  count ~ 1 + covariate_1 + sex + age_category + f(ID, model = "bym", graph = vecinos, scale.model = TRUE),

where the graph was obtained using sp::poly2nb.

I'm not sure if I've got the internal mechanics right. I don't know how INLA matches the graph with the data frame. My guess is that it uses the covariate you want to apply the Besag-York-Mollié model to, so that in this case, since ID has the same number of unique values as the number of nodes in the graph, it simply matches the first value to the first node, which in turn would mean that the model produces similar fitted values within each polygon (which was actually the case when I tried it), and I can just average the results per aerial unit, and then just join the results to the original spatial polygons data frame, but I don't have any certainty that that's what INLA is doing.

What's the correct way to specify the model?

Thank you,
Bernardo

messages.subject: joint model for point pattern data
messages.subject_clean: joint model for point pattern data
messages.body_plain:
Hi

I have three types of observations, which are point pattern data.
I use log gaussian cox processes (LGCP) to analyze each category separately, and I have found that their spatial effects overlap.
So I prefer to analyze the spatial effects of sharing. Should I use the joint model, or maybe there is a joint LGCP? .

Any suggest or help will be very appreciated.

Best.

messages.subject: modelling recurrents events taking into account the order of the events!
messages.subject_clean: modelling recurrents events taking into account the order of the events!
messages.body_plain:
I used the SPDE models with INLA almost 2 years ago but I still don't understand why we have to put "0 + a0" in the formula.

                                                  formula <- inla.surv(times, Status) ~ 0 + a0 + Treatment + Age + Sex +  f(spatial, model=CoxSPDE)

Please, could someone to explain us under which condition "0+ a0" should be added to the formula and exactly how important it would be? Why can't we write like that...

                                                formula <- inla.surv(times, Status) ~   Treatment + Age + Sex +  f(spatial, model=CoxSPDE)

In addition, I would like to model recurrents events taking into account the order of the events. Could adding "f(Order, model="iid") in to model formula solve the problem?
Since the risk decreases according to the order of events, we can put "f(Order, model="ar1) ?

formula <- inla.surv(times, Status, subject) ~ Treatment + Age + Sex +  f(spatial, model=CoxSPDE) + f(Order, model="ar1")

Thank you in advance for your support, it would be a great pleasure to have the solution to my problem on this forum....

Kindly!
Abdoulaye

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] I am using a survey data from a 2-stage sample, is it not necessary to apply population weights using INLA?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] I am using a survey data from a 2-stage sample, is it not necessary to apply population weights using INLA?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chigozie,

Just to make sure we are talking about the same thing, survey-weights
are weights used on complex sampling which somehow try to correct
biases on the sampling. For example, you may sample the same number of
people in two different cities, but one city is a way bigger than the
other. So you change the "importance" of the participants from
different cities by giving weights that are proportional to the
population of the city they come from.

So you could use the weights parameters in the INLA function, but you
should do it with extra careful. First thing you should do is to
normalize your sampling weights such as they add up to the sample size
and not as the population size as it is usual in complex sampling. In
complex sampling is it used to leave the weights as they are and
correct the variance estimators after, we don't do that in Bayesian
inference, and this is why you should normalize your sampling weights.

When you include the  sampling weights in the weights parameter in
INLA you are actually changing the likelihood to a pseudo-likelihood
instead, and therefore you are no longer doing inference on the
posterior distribution but on the pseudo-posterior distribution of the
parameters. If that is OK for you go ahead. The second issue you
should worry is to make sure you have proper priors, otherwise it is
not guaranteed the your pseudo-posterior is proper.

Another approach, using INLA, was proposed by Vandendijck et al (2016)
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2211675316300690

Cheers,
Leo Bastos
Associate researcher at Oswaldo Cruz Foundation, Brazil
Research Fellow at LSHTM, UK
Twitter: @leosbastos

On Mon, 2019-08-05 at 07:54 -0700, Abdoulaye GUINDO wrote:
>
> Now there remains the question about the DIC infinite of my model
> that is still unresolved. Do you have any idea?

This is usually an overflow issue, mainly because of an weakly indentified model.

Like DIC would require an integral like

	\int  exp(x) dx

and if the marginal variance of x is large, then exp(x) at the upper limit
might evaluate to infinity, giving an infinite DIC.

you can check the local dic,

> r=inla(y~1,data = data.frame(y=1:10), control.compute = list(dic=TRUE))
> r$dic$local.dic
 [1] 6.933122948 5.876833720 5.084616798 4.556472184 4.292399875 4.292399873
 [7] 4.556472178 5.084616789 5.876833707 6.933122931

and you can check what goes to Inf and maybe you see in the data what causes this.

--

Hello,

in reading the help file for inla.spde2.pcmatern, I find that it states:

>  The practical approach for this in INLA is to require the user to indirectly specify these hyperparameters through
>
> P(ρ < ρ_0) = p_ρ
>
> and
>
> P(σ > σ_0) = p_σ
>
> where the user specifies the lower tail quantile and probability for the range (ρ_0 and p_ρ) and the upper tail quantile and probability for the standard deviation (σ_0 and α_σ).

However, I had always understood them as, for example,
P(ρ < 500) = 0.95 meaning that the probability that the range is below 500 is 95% and
P(σ > 0.5) = 0.01 meaning that the probability that sigma is smaller than 0.5 is 1%.

If this is correct, shouldn't the help file say that we specify the higher tail quantile and probability for the range, and the lower for the st dev? Or is there something I am getting very wrong?

Cheers,

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] inla.spde2.pcmatern prior interpretation from the R help file
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] inla.spde2.pcmatern prior interpretation from the R help file
messages.body_plain:
Hi Virginia,

the "lower tail" is linked to the probability of being below a certain
quantile, and "upper tail" is linked to the probability of being above
a quantile, regardless of whether those probabilities are large or
small; hence, the quantiles may be in either the left tail, middle, or
right tail of the distribution, as determined by the given
probability.
Normally, both probabilities in the pcmatern definition are set to
_small_ values, e.g. (in a modified version of your example)
  P(ρ < 5) = 0.01 meaning that the probability that the range is below
5 is 1% and
  P(σ > 0.5) = 0.01 meaning that the probability that sigma is larger
than than 0.5 is 1%.
Note that for the range we control the probability of the lower
quantile (left tail) and for sigma we control the upper quantile
(right tail).

So one might ask why we control different tails for the two
parameters. The reason is that the "base model" corresponds to
infinite range and zero standard deviation.
By using a small probability for the two given tails we are therefore
specifying how far away we think it's unlikely the model should be
from the base model, which essentially "ties down" the model in "both
ends".  (Other conventions for how to choose the priors are also
possible, but this is the one that motivates the specification system
for the inla.spde2.pcmatern function.)

Finn

>>

>>
>> where the user specifies the lower tail quantile and probability for the range (ρ_0 and p_ρ) and the upper tail quantile and probability for the standard deviation (σ_0 and α_σ).

messages.body_plain:
Could I ask a few questions concerning the indices needed
to run an ar1 replicated model in a longitudinal setting?

The model will have for its random effects specification:

f(idx.ts, model="ar1",  replicate=idx.repl)

where idx.ts is an index of the time series, and idx.repl
is the index for the replicates. My questions concern how to
construct these two indices, given the structure of the data.
The story I have in mind is where I indivs are observed at T
times.

CASE 1 : the data is stacked by individuals, then by time.

Indiv      Time
=====   ====
1           1
1           2
1           3
2           1
2           2
2           3

In this case, I think that idx.ts is 1 2 3  1 2 3 ...
and idx.repl is 1 1 1  2 2 2 ...
Is this right?

CASE 2 - same data, but stacked by times, then indivs

Indiv      Time
=====   ====
1           1
2           1
3           1
1           2
2           2
3           2

In this case is idx.ts = 1 1 1   2 2 2 ...  and
idx.repl = 1 2 3   1 2 3  ... ? If not, what should
they be?

CASE 3 - Like case 1 except that indiv 2 is observed only
at times 1 and 3 (in this case I also show indiv 3):

Indiv      Time
=====   ====
1           1
1           2
1           3
2           1
2           3
3           1
3           2
3           3

Here I'm stumped. Should the idx.ts be 1 2 3  1 3   1 2 3 ...
and then idx.repl = 1 1 1   2 2  3 3 3  ...  or what?

Final question: am I correct that if the indivs and times
had been identified as 0,1,2 .. (instead of 1,2,3 ...)
or the times as years (1990, 1991, ...) then
the indices in the f-specification must still start from 1?
Or could they be zero-based or match the years?

Basically, I'm not sure I understand what the two indices
are supposed to be revealing. If anyone could set me
straight I'd be most grateful.

In other settings, I see WAIC calculated as the result of simulations from the posterior, with a standard error often provided to help determine whether differences in WAIC between models are meaningful (e.g., with the LOO package).

Is this because, as a deterministic system, there only is one possible WAIC value for an INLA posterior?  When I repeat the model run, the calculated WAIC value appears to be identical.

Or, should I be resampling the provided “waic” pointwise values to generate a standard error around the reported value?

Thanks.

Hello
I am new to R-INLA. I have a dataset spanning 100 polygons (I.e. for each postal codes -> lattice data). I am running a besag model for the regional component with a rw1 for the time component

response ~ 1 +f(region, model = 'bym', graph = adj) + f(time, model = 'rw1') + f(time.unstr, model = 'iid')

following Biangiardo (2013) (Spatial and spatio-temporal models with R-INLA).

The example I was following used an adjacency matrix, and it actually works fine. However, I now want to include a seasonal effect and the examples I find for this (https://ourcodingclub.github.io/2018/12/04/inla.html) used a mesh and stacking. My questions:

1) Do I need to stack my relatively simple model setup?
2) Do I need a mesh if I have an adjacency matrix (lattice data, not point data)?

I see why a mesh is necessary for point-data, but I don't understand what the mesh does in the case of lattice data (if it is needed).

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] mesh and adjacency matrix
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] mesh and adjacency matrix
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

1) Adjacency graphs are for discretised space, and meshes are for continuous space, so no, you don’t need to involve a mesh.
2) stacks are never strictly needed, they are just convenient when constructing some types of model. In your case you can probably make it work without them, since you just need to construct the “group” index vector. However, you can also use stacks in a simplified way to the mesh models; essentially just ignore most of the mesh related stuff and replace the mesh.index output with your regular graph index vector when calling inla.stack;
 Alternatively, you can even call inla.spde.make.A without a mesh; instead, supply “index” and “group”. This needs to be combined with inla.spde.make.index to make the canonical index vectors for the latent model.

Finn

I noticed that this post from ~ two years ago as I am having similar problems to those described by Anna.

I'm trying to run some land cost data through SLM, SDM and SEM models. While the models all converge successfully I am struggling to obtain predictions from the SEM model for un-modeled areas, which seems to provide the best fit for the data. As per suggestions in a couple vignettes, I included the relevant covariates for the locations where I wanted to make predictions and provided response values of NAs for the model. However, using the semm1$summary.fitted.values$mean code just seems to spit out predictions that are identical to the known values. I know one suggestion in this post was to look at some jags code for linear combinations. Have any other solutions been uncovered since that time? Either way, is there example code somewhere that I could use to learn a bit more about how to do this? The previous post mentions code in a jags GitHub location but I couldn't seem to find a relevant code line there either (although I could very well just not be looking for the right thing).
Input appreciated.
Thanks,
Kaylan

Hi,

>
> I'm trying to run some land cost data through SLM, SDM and SEM models. While the models all converge successfully I am struggling to obtain predictions from the SEM model for un-modeled areas, which seems to provide the best fit for the data. As per suggestions in a couple vignettes, I included the relevant covariates for the locations where I wanted to make predictions and provided response values of NAs for the model. However, using the semm1$summary.fitted.values$mean code just seems to spit out predictions that are identical to the known values.

This is actually a ‘feature’ of how the model is defined as the variance of the Gaussian likelihood is close to zero.

> I know one suggestion in this post was to look at some jags code for linear combinations. Have any other solutions been uncovered since that time?

This is something that we need to check in detail and probably address it in the paper where we describe the slm latent effect...

> Either way, is there example code somewhere that I could use to learn a bit more about how to do this? The previous post mentions code in a jags GitHub location but I couldn't seem to find a relevant code line there either (although I could very well just not be looking for the right thing).

The package is now called SEMCMC (as it includes the possibility of fitting models with Stan in addition to JAGS). Hence, this code should work:

devtools::install_github("becarioprecario/SEMCMC")
library(SEMCMC)

The vignette does not seem to be available using vignette() but you can browse it in the local installation or directly on GitHub.

Best,

Virgilio

messages.body_plain:
Dear Alfred,

I prefer to use inla.make.lincombs(). It takes a named list. The names must be identical to the name of the parameter. In case of a fixed effect, use a vector (one element per contrast). In case of a random effect, use a matrix (one row per contrast, one column for each random effect index).
You can name the contrasts by setting names to the output of inla.make.lincombs().

So I'm testing this model on simulated data generated from a random slope and intercept model with two groups with the same underlying mean function differing by an additive constant. messages.subject: Is MCMC Obsolete?
messages.subject_clean: Is MCMC Obsolete?
messages.body_plain:
I'm just entering the exciting world of INLA (and Bayesian spatial analysis in general); the possibilities seem limitless!  I hope to post some other questions as soon as I'm able to formulate them properly, but for right now, my question is this:  does the Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation make Monte Carlo methods (e.g., Markov Chain Monte Carlo, MCMC) obsolete?

If the INLA approximation does just as well as sampling from the posterior distribution, and does it much faster, why would anyone ever use MCMC?  Put another way, is there really a free lunch?  I guess the answer to this question hinges on how accurate the approximation is.  One paper (Carroll, R., et al. 2015. "Comparing INLA to OpenBUGS for hierarchial Poisson modeling in disease mapping <https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4633705/>," Spatial and Spatiotemporal Epidemiology, 0: 45-54) conducted a simulation study and concluded that R-INLA's default settings did not recover the true parameters as accurately as BUGS, but that after fine-tuning the parameters, R-INLA performed comparably to BUGS.  Is anyone aware of other studies like this?  Thoughts?

Many thanks to Håvard Rue, his team, and his students for developing R-INLA and providing such helpful online tools for learning and using it!

Regards,
David Crow,
California Department of Public Health

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Is MCMC Obsolete?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Is MCMC Obsolete?
messages.body_plain:
There are room for both, both MCMC and INLA, and one does not rule out
the other. For latent Gaussian models (LGMs), then there is so much
structure that can be made use of, and this is what INLA does. So you
can see it as a special approximation/solution for a restricted set of
models, whereas MCMC is a generic approach for 'all' models.

If MCMC is ``needed'' for those models INLA can do well, that is
another issue, yes.

H

messages.body_plain:
OK after some tinkering I think I figured it out. I think the issue is that I forgot that the term f(time, method="rw2", replicate=id) has a sum-to-zero constraint so it couldn't model additive deviations from the group effects. To address this I added a random intercept term, so the model reads

y ~ factor(x) + f(time_x1, model="rw2") + f(time_x2, model="rw2") +

      f(id, model="iid") + f(time, model="rw2", replicate=id)

This yields estimates that agree with the random slope and intercept model without assuming linear random effects.

Incidentally, a model that works equally well is one using AR1 random effects:

y ~ factor(x) + f(time_x1, model="rw2") + f(time_x2, model="rw2") +

     f(time, model="ar1", replicate=id)

Here we don't need to have an "iid" effect since it's already incorporated into the "ar1" model.

I hope this is helpful to someone in the future. If I'm misunderstanding anything please let me know. Thanks for the help!

messages.subject_clean: Using posterior mean range for correlation plots
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I would like to visualise the autocorrelation of a dependent variable without considering any fixed covariates. This might seem strange to some, but it is relevant for my research. I am less certain about the next part though. Since there is little prior information to go on, I would build a model with an intercept and a barrier SGF based on an acceptable diffuse prior for range. Then I would use the approach described here <https://haakonbakka.bitbucket.io/btopic128.html#6_plotting_priors>, but using posterior mean range instead of a prior range to calculate the precision matrix for visualising the spatial autocorrelation. I have not yet found any clear arguments against this approach myself, but as I am quite new to INLA and the Bayesian framework I would be grateful to get some feedback if I am making a mistake.

Thank you for your time,
Sam

messages.subject: robust Bayesian modeling
messages.subject_clean: robust Bayesian modeling
messages.body_plain:
I know there has been some effort made to incorporate student t distributions into INLA, and that it has been challenging.

I read with great interest this paper by Wang and Blei, http://www.cs.columbia.edu/~blei/papers/WangBlei2018.pdf, which contends that the better way to accomplish robust estimation is to set up exponential models with an additional localization parameter, and then set up a second likelihood to describe the probability of each observation, with its hyperparameter estimated by empirical bayes (or presumably some equivalent).  For a normal distribution, for example, the location parameter would get its own prior operating over each observation, which transforms the error distribution into the Student T.  The benefit is that the framework, once established, works for all types of exponential models (linear, logistic, poisson, etc.), with the difference on the front end being the “flag” of enabling robust estimation when it is desired, and under the hood, the parameterization of the second likelihood for the family in question to incorporate the localization option.  Worst case, the results come out the same, and best case, the results appear to be more robust.

Is this an approach that could be accommodated in INLA without violating any of its core assumptions, given INLA’s ability to handle multiple likelihoods? At least at a high level, this method sounds like the approach already taken to estimate measurement error, which seems to have been integrated successfully into the system.

As an alternative to the more ambitious idea above, at least for binary data, would it be possible for INLA to incorporate a robit option?  The probit and logit arguably are already special cases of the robit, and the robit would allow the degrees of freedom for the student T CDF to better accommodate outlier observations.

Some discussions of what this might look like, both generally and in Stan:

https://www.stat.purdue.edu/~chuanhai/teaching/Stat598A/robit.pdf

https://stackoverflow.com/questions/26447512/how-to-run-a-robit-model-in-stan

Jonathan

On Thu, 2019-08-22 at 23:04 -0500, Jonathan Judge wrote:
> I know there has been some effort made to incorporate student t
> distributions into INLA, and that it has been challenging.
>
> I read with great interest this paper by Wang and Blei,
> http://www.cs.columbia.edu/~blei/papers/WangBlei2018.pdf, which
> contends that the better way to accomplish robust estimation is to
> set up exponential models with an additional localization parameter,
> and then set up a second likelihood to describe the probability of
> each observation, with its hyperparameter estimated by empirical
> bayes (or presumably some equivalent).  For a normal distribution,
> for example, the location parameter would get its own prior operating
> over each observation, which transforms the error distribution into
> the Student T.  The benefit is that the framework, once established,
> works for all types of exponential models (linear, logistic, poisson,
> etc.), with the difference on the front end being the “flag” of
> enabling robust estimation when it is desired, and under the hood,
> the parameterization of the second likelihood for the family in
> question to incorporate the localization option.  Worst case, the
> results come out the same, and best case, the results appear to be
> more robust.
>
> Is this an approach that could be accommodated in INLA without
> violating any of its core assumptions, given INLA’s ability to handle
> multiple likelihoods? At least at a high level, this method sounds
> like the approach already taken to estimate measurement error, which
> seems to have been integrated successfully into the system.
>
> As an alternative to the more ambitious idea above, at least for
> binary data, would it be possible for INLA to incorporate a robit
> option?  The probit and logit arguably are already special cases of
> the robit, and the robit would allow the degrees of freedom for the
> student T CDF to better accommodate outlier observations.
>
> Some discussions of what this might look like, both generally and in
> Stan:
>
> https://www.stat.purdue.edu/~chuanhai/teaching/Stat598A/robit.pdf
> https://stackoverflow.com/questions/26447512/how-to-run-a-robit-model-in-stan
>
> Jonathan

I notice that you write the interval 20-24 and not the value 22. With the normal indexed RW2 model, you have to select a certain point that is representative of the interval (e.g. the median of the interval).

If you instead want the average of "rw2 at age 20, rw2 at age 21, rw2 at age 22, rw2 at age 23, rw2 at age 24", that can be done with the stack functionality and the A matrix.

Best,

messages.subject: INLA crashes when running on linux cluster supercomputer
messages.subject_clean: INLA crashes when running on linux cluster supercomputer
messages.body_plain:
Hi! I am very new to INLA and I want to apologize in advance if the question I have is very basic. I tried several solutions suggested in the forum, such as decreasing the number of threads, using "rw1" instead of "ar1", or reordering = "amdc", but nothing helped so far.

I am running a GLMM model (family binomial, logit link) in which the binary response variable y is a function of sin(time) and cos(time) defined as the minutes within a day; the model also contains an AR1 structure and a random component that depends on the variable id.  I have a large dataset in which id has 31 levels and time ranges from 1 to 89282 (total number of rows = 31 x 89282).

I started working on a subset of data that includes records from all the 31 sites, but only for one day (I recoded time so that it ranges from 1 to 1440 in the sample). I was able to run this model on my personal Windows machine (Windows 10 64-bit, RAM: 8GB, Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-45000 CPU @< 1.80GHz 2.40GHz) in about 40 minutes, and in another remote server (Windows Server 2016 Standard 64-bit, RAM: 4GB; Intel(R) Xeon(R) CPU E5-2695 v3 @ 2.30GHz 2.30GHz). I then tried to run the same script (with minor adjustment to include pardiso) on a Linux cluster supercomputer (Platform: x86_64-pc-linux-gnu (64-bit), CentOS Linux 7 (Core), running using 62GB) with the goal to increase the size of the subset and do some prior sensitivity analysis, but INLA crashes fairly soon. Unfortunately, even using verbose = TRUE I didn't get any information on what the problem is, so I used debug = TRUE. All the sistems are running the same version of R (3.6.0) and INLA.

I would like to know why the model is not running in the Linux cluster.

Below, code to reproduce the error using simulated data and the model I am running in the Linux cluster. Attached the output I get when running the script, with some debug information at the end.

I would very much appreciate any help and thank you in advance for any suggestion,
Fabiola

#' Load R libraries
#+ r libraries
rm(list=ls())
library(INLA)
library(brinla)
library(tidyverse)
library(tictoc)
library(data.table)
set.seed(129)
INLA:::inla.dynload.workaround() #to solve INLA's common issue when running in R
inla.setOption(pardiso.license = "pardiso.lic")
inla.setOption(mkl=TRUE)
inla.pardiso.check()

sessionInfo()

#' Simulate data
y_1min <- expand.grid(id = 1:31, time = 1:89282)
y_1min$y <- rbinom(n = nrow(y_1min), size = 1, prob = 0.0002547155) #prob from frequence of 1 in the real data

#' sin and cos predictors
y_1min$sin_pred <- sin((2*pi*y_1min$time)/(24 * 60))
y_1min$cos_pred <- cos((2*pi*y_1min$time)/(24 * 60))

y_1min <- y_1min %>% mutate(id = as.numeric(id), id2 = id, time = as.numeric(time), y = as.numeric(y))
dim(y_1min)
str(y_1min)
head(y_1min)

# create data subset
rand_time <- sample(x = min(y_1min$time):max(y_1min$time), size = 1)
rand_time
sample <- y_1min %>% group_by(id) %>% filter(time >= rand_time & time < (rand_time + 24*60*1))

length(unique(sample$id)); length(unique(sample$time)) #all id levels, contiguos times
max(sample$time)

# recode time to start from 1
sample$time2 <- sample$time - min(sample$time) + 1
dim(sample)
str(sample)
head(sample)

tic() #
mod_1day <- inla(y~1 + sin_pred + cos_pred + f(time2,model='ar1', replicate=id2) + f(id,model="iid"),
             data=sample, family="binomial", verbose=TRUE, num.threads=2, debug=TRUE,
control.inla = list(strategy = 'adaptive'),
control.compute=list(openmp.strategy="pardiso.parallel")
)
toc()

messages.subject: modeling the difference between two Binomials?
messages.subject_clean: modeling the difference between two Binomials?
messages.body_plain:
Hi INLA community,

I'm new to INLA, coming from Stan. In Stan we have a model:

Y_i^treatment ~ Binomial(N_i^treatment, p_i^treatment)
Y_i^control ~ Binomial(N_i^control, p_i^control)

p_i^treatment - p_i^control ~ Normal(X_i * beta, sigma)

where X_i * beta is a multilevel model.

But our Stan model fits too slowly for our purposes.

Is this likelihood possible to implement in INLA?

Thanks so much!
Shira

I agree with Haakon.

I would guess what you mean is that you have a joint model, one for
treatment and one for control

so

y^t ~ treatment
y^c ~ control

and then you want to impose a model for the difference as well

y^t ~ treatment - 1/2 * difference
y^c ~ control   + 1/2 * difference

where the 'difference' is the difference model

this is on the logit/probit scale.

messages.subject: non-matching units in a BYM model
messages.subject_clean: non-matching units in a BYM model
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have successfully run a BYM model using the following syntax for the spatial term:

f(as.numeric(PROP_IDB), model = "bym", graph = matrixGraph)
where "PROP_IDB" includes 270 unique IDs for parcels (polygons having different areas).

However, my data set has 5670 observations spread across the parcels, so, there is more than 1 observation for each parcel.

Since spatial units don't match with sampling units, how should I interpret the outcomes of the BYM model?, should I interpret the spatial errors estimated for the parcels as averaged errors using the observations within the same parcel?

Thank you very much in advance.

Juanmi
